Research note · US equity industries · Kenneth French data library

Industry All Weather

Can Bridgewater's four-environment risk balance be built from equity industries alone? We classify French industries by growth and inflation sensitivity, build four quadrant portfolios and combine them.

Evaluation window Jan 1965 – Aug 2026 (740 months, monthly rebalanced, before costs) · industry data CRSP 2026-08 · macro: FRED GDPC1, CPIAUCSL

  1. The macro classification is real. Every quadrant portfolio earns its best return relative to the market in its own regime. With the judgement-based classification (a) the diagonal excess returns are +1.5% / +6.2% / +7.1% / +5.4% a year; with regressions re-estimated out-of-sample they are still +4.0% / +3.1% / +2.5% / +4.5%.
  2. The All Weather combination beats the market modestly. On 48 industries, equal weights everywhere: CAGR 11.7% vs 10.8%, Sharpe 0.50 vs 0.46, alpha 1.1% a year. Risk-based weights (ERC inside and across quadrants) lift the Sharpe ratio to 0.53 and cut the maximum drawdown to -47%.
  3. It does not deliver Bridgewater-style crash protection. Beta is 0.98 and correlation 0.95. Balancing industries only diversifies the part of returns that is relative to the market (tracking error 5.2%). Market-wide crashes hit almost in full: 1973–74 -45% (market -47%), 2007–09 -49% (-50%).
  4. It shines when the market is concentrated in one regime bet: 2000–02 -7% vs -45%, 2022 -16% vs -25%. It lags when one regime's winners dominate cap weights, as with mega-cap tech after 2011.
  5. Judgement beats regression. The macro view (a) gives the best Sharpe ratio at every granularity except 10 industries. Full-sample regressions (b) agree with (a) on 60% of the 48 industries. Out-of-sample regressions (b-OOS) only roughly match the market's Sharpe ratio, because t-statistics of 1–2 make the quadrant labels noisy.
  6. Granularity matters little. From 5 to 49 industries the Sharpe ratio of (a) ERC/ERC stays in a 0.51–0.53 band. What matters is the regime structure, not the number of industries. Equal-weighting all industries gets worse as the set gets finer, while All Weather does not.

1All Weather in brief, and how we translate it

Bridgewater's All Weather portfolio, launched in 1996, starts from the view that asset prices move when growth and inflation differ from what is discounted. Each can come in above or below expectations, giving four environments. Each asset class is biased toward some of them: equities and credit like rising growth, nominal bonds like falling growth and falling inflation, and commodities and inflation-linked bonds like rising inflation. All Weather holds a portfolio for each environment and gives them equal risk, using leverage on low-volatility assets, so it does not have to forecast which environment comes next.

Inflation risingInflation falling Growth rising
G↑ I↑ · reflationAsset classes: commodities, EM credit, linkers. Our industries: steel, machinery, mines, paper, banks.
G↑ I↓ · goldilocksAsset classes: equities, corporate credit. Our industries: tech, autos, retail, restaurants, apparel.
Growth falling
G↓ I↑ · stagflationAsset classes: linkers, gold, commodities. Our industries: gold, oil, agriculture, food, tobacco, defence.
G↓ I↓ · disinflationary bustAsset classes: nominal bonds. Our industries: utilities, telecom, drugs, healthcare, insurance.

Here the investable universe is only US equity industries. So each industry is classified by how its return in excess of the equity market responds to growth and inflation. Quadrant portfolios are long-only industry baskets, and All Weather is a fully invested, unlevered mix of the four.

This changes what the exercise can achieve. Every industry carries a market beta near one, so balancing them diversifies the regime-driven relative returns and leaves the market factor untouched. Bridgewater's version gets most of its crash protection from bonds. Ours can only beat the market by tilting away from whichever regime bet the cap-weighted index happens to be concentrated in.

2Measuring growth and inflation regimes

Growth is year-on-year real GDP growth; inflation is year-on-year CPI inflation (quarterly average of monthly CPI). Bridgewater frames regimes relative to expectations. Without a long consensus-forecast history, we use the quarter-on-quarter change in those YoY rates as the surprise proxy: growth is "rising" when YoY growth accelerates. From 1948Q2 to 2026Q2 the 313 quarters split 69 / 78 / 94 / 72 across G↑I↑ / G↑I↓ / G↓I↑ / G↓I↓, and the regime changes in 61% of quarters. That is why a static, balanced portfolio makes sense: the regime is hard to time.

3Classifying industries

(a) Macro-economic view

Each industry gets a judgement score of ±1 or ±2 on growth and on inflation, based on its business economics: commodity exposure, pricing power, demand elasticity, cash-flow duration and rate sensitivity. Gold miners are the textbook stagflation hedge (G↓ I↑). Oil follows the 1973/79/2022 supply-shock pattern (G↓ I↑). Steel and machinery are capex-cycle commodity producers (G↑ I↑). Tech, autos and restaurants are long-duration or discretionary (G↑ I↓). Utilities, telecoms and drugs are bond proxies (G↓ I↓). The sign pair sets the quadrant. Scores were written down before looking at any regression.

(b) Regression view

Quarterly industry return minus market return is regressed on the standardised changes in YoY GDP growth and YoY CPI inflation (both entered together, clipped at ±3σ to contain the 2020 swing, Newey-West t-stats with 4 lags, 1948Q2–2026Q2). The signs of the two betas set the quadrant. A strictly out-of-sample version (b-OOS) re-estimates every January on an expanding window, using data only through Q3 of the prior year.

If a quadrant would be empty (only at coarse levels), the industry with the highest score in that direction is borrowed into it. The chart shows both views at once: position is the regression t-statistics (b), colour is the macro view (a). Industries whose colour matches their corner are the 60% where the two agree.

The regressions support the textbook macro calls: coal, oil, steel, machinery, gold and agriculture load positively on inflation surprises, while restaurants, retail, apparel and consumer services are hurt. The surprises are interesting too. Banks behave defensively rather than as reflation trades. Utilities and insurers carry slightly positive inflation betas once the market is netted out. Construction and building materials act as rate-sensitive housing plays (I↓) rather than real-asset plays.

4Does the classification work?

The direct test: in which realised regimes does each quadrant portfolio beat the market? If the classification is right, the diagonal should be the best cell in each row. For (a) this is a genuine test, since the scores were set from economics rather than fitted. For (b) in-sample the diagonal is partly built in, which is why the out-of-sample panel matters.

All three panels have a positive diagonal. The macro view gives the cleanest pattern: its stagflation basket returns +7.1% a year over the market in stagflation quarters and −3.5% in goldilocks quarters. In the macro view the reflation (G↑ I↑) quadrant is the weakest, because industrial cyclicals respond to growth more than to inflation. Over the long run the quadrant portfolios drift a long way apart against the market. That dispersion is what an equal-risk mix diversifies.

Base case: industries equal-weighted within each quadrant, quadrants equal-weighted in All Weather, rebalanced monthly. The table adds the equal-weighted average of all 48 industries as a benchmark. The pattern is clear. When the market falls on a concentrated regime bet, All Weather protects. The 2000–02 bust was a goldilocks/tech unwind and the 2022 sell-off was an inflation shock; in both, the stagflation and defensive quadrants offset the losers. In systemic sell-offs (1973–74, 2008, March 2020) every industry falls together and the quadrant structure cannot help. In March 2020 the cyclical and energy-heavy quadrants fell more than the market. Bonds, which All Weather lacks here, are the missing hedge.

The macro-view portfolio beats the market on average in all four regimes, most in disinflationary busts and stagflation, and roughly matches it in reflation. That is what "all weather" should mean for a relative-to-market portfolio.

Risk-based weighting helps consistently but modestly: about +0.01 Sharpe from IV or ERC within quadrants and another +0.01 from ERC across them, which also takes 2–3 points off the maximum drawdown. The two steps add about the same Sharpe, but only ERC across quadrants reduces drawdowns. It cuts the growth quadrants to about 21% of capital each and raises the two growth-down quadrants to about 29% each. That is the true risk-parity step, and the equity analogue of Bridgewater levering up bonds. Turnover stays around 20% a year for all schemes. The classification choice, (a) vs (b) vs (b-OOS), matters about twice as much as the weighting scheme.

More industries do not mean better macro balance. The macro view is stable from 5 to 49 (Sharpe 0.51–0.53), and the 17-industry set has the shallowest drawdown. The regression views are less stable. With few industries, a single misclassified sector moves a whole quadrant, and the 5- and 10-industry sets need a borrowed industry to fill the stagflation quadrant. With many, the t-statistics are noisier. The equal-weighted benchmark gets worse with granularity, because finer sets over-weight small cyclical niches. The quadrant structure stops that from happening, which is a direct way to see its diversification value.

8Conclusions and next steps

  • The growth/inflation framework transfers well to equity industries as a relative-value map. Industries sort reliably into regime winners and losers, and an economically reasoned classification holds up better than a fitted one.
  • An industry-only All Weather is a better-diversified equity portfolio: Sharpe 0.50–0.53 vs 0.46, slightly smaller drawdowns, strong protection against concentration unwinds. It is not a multi-asset crash hedge.
  • Prefer ERC across quadrants, the step that actually equalises regime risk, together with the macro classification. Industry granularity is a second-order choice; 17–48 industries is a sensible range.

Suggested extensions. (1) Isolate the regime overlay: long each quadrant, short the market, ERC across the four spreads. This is a market-neutral macro factor that could sit alongside bonds and commodities in a true multi-asset All Weather. (2) Measure surprises against expectations (Survey of Professional Forecasters, breakevens) rather than as changes in realised data. (3) Use time-varying, shrunk betas for (b), Bayesian-blended with the (a) priors. (4) Lever to a target volatility and add transaction costs.

9Method and data notes

  • Returns: Kenneth French value-weighted monthly industry portfolios (5…49), CRSP 2026-08 vintage. Market = Mkt-RF + RF from the Fama-French research factors. Missing values (−99.99) are treated as not investable.
  • Eligibility: an industry is held from month t only if it has 36 consecutive months of returns to t−1 (for example, Gold, Soda, Guns and FabPr enter in the mid-1960s). Quadrant portfolios are built from 1931 to give the across-quadrant risk models history. All results are reported over Jan 1965 – Aug 2026, the window where the out-of-sample classification exists.
  • Look-ahead: weights use only past returns. Classification (a) and (b) are static over the full sample. (b) is in-sample by construction, and (b-OOS) is the honest benchmark for it. (a) uses no fitted data, but it is written with today's knowledge of industry economics.
  • Not included: transaction costs (turnover is about 20% a year one-way, so cost drag is small), leverage, taxes.
  • Code: allweather/ package (data, classify, portfolio, analytics, figures), run.py (study grid), report.py and build_html.py (this page).
Sources: Kenneth R. French Data Library (Dartmouth Tuck); FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis; Bridgewater Associates, "The All Weather Story". Past performance of back-tested portfolios is hypothetical and does not include costs.
